details:
**Interpreter of Maladies**
Lahiri's 1999 debut short story collection, which won the 2000 Pulitzer Prize for Fiction. It is her most common giveaway, and it contains stories such as "A Temporary Matter," "When Mr. Pirzada Came to Dine," "Sexy," "This Blessed House," and "The Third and Final Continent."

**Mr. Kapasi, Mrs. Das, and Bobby attacked by monkeys**
The title story of Interpreter of Maladies follows Mr. Kapasi, a tour guide who also works as an interpreter for a doctor whose patients speak Gujarati. While driving the Indian-American Das family to the Sun Temple at Konarak, he grows infatuated with Mrs. Das, but at the end her son Bobby is swarmed by monkeys after she carelessly drops puffed rice, and Mr. Kapasi rescues him.

**Mrs. Das's secret (Bobby is illegitimate)**
In "Interpreter of Maladies," Mrs. Das confesses to Mr. Kapasi that her son Bobby was fathered by another man during an affair, a secret she has kept for eight years. She hopes he can "interpret" her malady, but he only asks whether what she feels is really pain or guilt, which offends her. The story opens with Mr. and Mrs. Das bickering at a tea stall over who will take their daughter Tina to the toilet.

**"Sexy" (Miranda, Dev, and the Mapparium)**
A story in Interpreter of Maladies in which Miranda has an affair with Dev, a married Bengali man who whispers that she is "sexy" inside the Mapparium, a walk-in stained-glass globe at the Christian Science center in Boston. She breaks off the affair after Rohin, the seven-year-old boy she babysits, defines "sexy" as "loving someone you don't know."

**"A Temporary Matter" (Shoba and Shukumar)**
The opening story of Interpreter of Maladies, about a married couple grieving their stillborn baby. During a series of nightly scheduled power outages, they confess secrets to each other by candlelight; Shukumar admits he cheated on an Oriental Civilization exam and tore a model's photo out of a magazine, and finally reveals that he held their dead son and knows his sex. He had been at an academic conference in Baltimore during the birth.

**The Namesake (Gogol Ganguli)**
Lahiri's first novel (2003), about Gogol Ganguli, the son of Bengali immigrants in Massachusetts, who resents his unusual name and legally changes it to Nikhil. He dates Maxine Ratliff, breaks up with her after his father dies, and later marries his childhood acquaintance Moushumi, who cheats on him with Dimitri Desjardins.

**Ashoke's train accident and "The Overcoat"**
In The Namesake, Gogol's father Ashoke survives a train derailment in India because rescuers notice him clutching (or waving) pages of Nikolai Gogol's short story "The Overcoat." In gratitude he names his son after the Russian author. Ashoke later studies engineering at MIT and dies while working in Cleveland, a departure Gogol misses because he spends the night with his girlfriend.

**"When Mr. Pirzada Came to Dine"**
A story in Interpreter of Maladies narrated by Lilia, a young girl in New England whose family hosts Mr. Pirzada, a professor from Dacca, during the 1971 war that created Bangladesh. Each night she eats a candy he gives her and prays for the safety of his family; after he returns home and writes that they are safe, she throws the candies away.

**The Lowland (Subhash, Udayan, and Gauri)**
Lahiri's 2013 novel, about two brothers in Calcutta. Udayan joins the Naxalite (Maoist) movement and is killed by police, and his brother Subhash, a graduate student in Rhode Island, marries Udayan's pregnant widow Gauri and brings her to America. Subhash has an affair with Holly, whom he meets on the beach with her son Joshua.

**Unaccustomed Earth**
Lahiri's 2008 second story collection, whose title comes from a passage in Nathaniel Hawthorne's "The Custom-House." In the title story, Ruma, living in Seattle, is visited by her widowed father, whose postcard to another woman reveals his new relationship. The collection also contains "Only Goodness," in which Rahul drops out of Cornell, becomes an alcoholic, and ends up working at a laundromat, and "Nobody's Business," in which the graduate student Paul helps his housemate Sang break off her relationship with the deceitful Farouk.

**Hema and Kaushik (death in a tsunami)**
The linked three-story sequence that closes Unaccustomed Earth. Kaushik becomes a war photojournalist and dies in the 2004 Indian Ocean tsunami while staying at a resort in Thailand.

**"The Third and Final Continent"**
The final story of Interpreter of Maladies, narrated by a Bengali man who moves from London to Boston and rents a room from Mrs. Croft, a 103-year-old woman on Massachusetts Avenue. She insists he say "Splendid!" about the American flag planted on the moon, and later his wife Mala joins him in America.

**"This Blessed House" (Twinkle and Sanjeev)**
A story in Interpreter of Maladies about a newlywed couple in Connecticut. Twinkle delights in the Christian trinkets left by previous owners, such as a statue of the Virgin Mary and a silver bust of Jesus, while her husband Sanjeev is irritated by them.

**"The Treatment of Bibi Haldar"**
A story in Interpreter of Maladies about a young woman in Calcutta afflicted by a mysterious illness, whose relatives believe marriage will cure her. She is "cured" after she becomes pregnant by an unknown man.

**Writing in Italian ("Teach Yourself Italian," Roman Stories)**
Lahiri moved to Rome and began writing in Italian, explaining the shift in the essay "Teach Yourself Italian" and the book In Other Words. Her later Italian-language works include the novel Whereabouts and the collection Roman Stories, which contains "The Boundary." She teaches at Princeton.
